raw_text:
# Angiotensin Receptor-Neprilysin Inhibition in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

Heart failure (HF) remains a major global public health challenge, historically managed by neurohormonal antagonists targeting the overactivated renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and sympathetic nervous system. The introduction of sacubitril/valsartan, a first-in-class angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), represented a major paradigm shift in cardiovascular medicine [1]. This therapeutic agent combines RAAS blockade with the enhancement of the protective endogenous natriuretic peptide system. 

## Clinical Efficacy in HFrEF and Tolerability

The landmark PARADIGM-HF trial established the therapeutic superiority of sacubitril/valsartan over the previous gold standard of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibition in patients with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) [2]. In this double-blind trial, 8,442 ambulatory HFrEF patients were randomized to receive either sacubitril/valsartan (200 mg twice daily) or enalapril (10 mg twice daily). The trial was halted prematurely due to an overwhelming clinical benefit, demonstrating a 20% reduction in the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization (hazard ratio [HR] 0.80, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.73–0.87, p<0.001) [2]. 

Subsequent clinical trials explored its safety and efficacy in alternative environments. While PARADIGM-HF examined chronic, stable outpatients, the PIONEER-HF trial assessed the in-hospital initiation of sacubitril/valsartan in patients stabilized after an episode of acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) [3]. Initiating ARNI therapy in this acute, vulnerable setting led to a significantly greater reduction in N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) levels and a lower rate of post-discharge rehospitalization than enalapril [3]. Furthermore, researchers sought to determine if these clinical benefits extended to patients with higher left ventricular ejection fractions (LVEF), leading to the PARAGON-HF trial in patients with heart failure and preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) [4].

The safety and tolerability of sacubitril/valsartan have been thoroughly characterized. In PARADIGM-HF, patients assigned to the ARNI arm experienced a higher incidence of symptomatic hypotension but fewer instances of severe renal impairment, hyperkalemia, or cough compared to the enalapril arm [5]. Detailed renal analyses confirmed that the long-term decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was significantly slower with sacubitril/valsartan than with ACE inhibition [6]. In addition, patients with diabetes and HFrEF showed glycemic benefits, exhibiting a slower increase in HbA1c levels over time with ARNI therapy [7]. 

In acute settings, the reduction of NT-proBNP occurred rapidly without compromising clinical safety parameters [8]. However, the efficacy of ARNI is not universal across all cohorts. In advanced, end-stage HFrEF, the LIFE trial showed that sacubitril/valsartan did not offer superior clinical or biomarker benefit compared to valsartan alone [9]. Meanwhile, trials like PARAGLIDE-HF assessed the safety and efficacy of ARNI initiation in stabilized patients with ejection fractions above 40%, showing favorable biomarker outcomes [10]. In the post-myocardial infarction cohort, however, the PARADISE-MI trial did not demonstrate a significant reduction in cardiovascular death or incident heart failure compared to ramipril [11].

## Efficacy across the Ejection Fraction Spectrum

Despite neutral primary results in specific clinical settings, a pooled analysis of the PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF trials confirmed that the therapeutic benefits of sacubitril/valsartan exist along a continuous spectrum of LVEF, showing particular clinical benefit in patients with mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF) and in women [12]. 

These clinical trials have heavily influenced contemporary guideline recommendations. Both the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology/Heart Failure Society of America (AHA/ACC/HFSA) [13] and the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) [14] guidelines now issue a Class I recommendation for sacubitril/valsartan as a primary first-line treatment for patients with HFrEF, recommending it either as initial therapy or as a replacement for an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB).

## Myocardial Remodeling and Long-Term Impact

The physiological benefits of sacubitril/valsartan are closely linked to favorable cardiac structural remodeling. The PROVE-HF study demonstrated that initiating sacubitril/valsartan led to rapid, sustained reductions in NT-proBNP, which directly correlated with improvements in LVEF and reductions in left ventricular and left atrial volume indexes [15]. Additionally, the EVALUATE-HF trial showcased positive changes in central aortic stiffness and left ventricular structure [16]. These trials supported findings from earlier biomarker substudies of PARADIGM-HF, which linked reductions in NT-proBNP with superior clinical outcomes and less progressive cardiac damage [17]. Furthermore, the risk of developing hyperkalemia remained significantly lower during ARNI therapy, even when combined with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists [18].

The long-term impact of sacubitril/valsartan on clinical stability is extensive. In addition to preventing first events, the ARNI significantly reduces total recurrent HF hospitalizations [19], with projections estimating a lifetime survival benefit of up to 2.5 years [20]. Cognitive function was also monitored due to theoretical concerns regarding neprilysin-mediated amyloid-beta accumulation; however, a dedicated clinical trial confirmed that cognitive function was preserved over mid-term follow-up [21]. Health-related quality of life was consistently improved [22], and these benefits were maintained regardless of patient age [23]. In addition, in patients with HFpEF, sacubitril/valsartan slowed the rate of kidney function decline [24].

In terms of clinical execution, the TRANSITION trial confirmed that early initiation of sacubitril/valsartan—either in-hospital or shortly after discharge—is safe, well-tolerated, and feasible [25]. Integration of the ARNI alongside modern therapies, such as the soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator vericiguat studied in the VICTORIA trial [26], highlights its central status as a foundational pillar of modern medical management, regardless of baseline therapies [27]. Titration strategies are also highly versatile; the TITRATION trial demonstrated that both 3-week and 6-week up-titration schemes are highly effective in achieving target doses [28]. Pediatric cohorts have also been investigated, with the PANORAMA-HF trial confirming the safety, pharmacokinetics, and clinical utility of sacubitril/valsartan in children with heart failure [29]. Finally, clinical studies indicate that the systemic benefits of ARNI therapy may be partially mediated by favorable reductions in sympathetic nervous system activity and improved heart rate stability [30].
